docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
Ory Kratos (commit b86338d) is the identity server. It runs the registration flow, checks the input, and stores identities and sessions. The UI is a separate web app that only renders the forms Kratos describes.

  • Kratos (public API): http://127.0.0.1:4433
  • UI: http://127.0.0.1:4455

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Browser opens the sign-up page: GET :4455/registration.
  2. UI has no flow yet, so it redirects the browser to Kratos to start one: GET :4433/self-service/registration/browser.
  3. Kratos creates a registration flow, sets a CSRF cookie, and redirects back to the UI with the flow ID: /registration?flow=<id>.

  4. UI fetches the flow from Kratos (GET /self-service/registration/flows?id=<id>) and shows the profile form. The flow describes the form (server-driven UI, trimmed):

    {
  "id": "faaa3fc0-0203-4085-ac76-3b6ca668908a",
  "type": "browser",
  "state": "choose_method",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-12T01:10:49Z",
  "ui": {
    "action": "http://127.0.0.1:4433/self-service/registration?flow=faaa3fc0-…",
    "method": "POST",
    "nodes": [
      { "attributes": { "name": "csrf_token", "type": "hidden", "value": "<token>" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.email", "type": "email", "required": true } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.first", "type": "text" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.last", "type": "text" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "method", "type": "submit", "value": "profile" } }
    ]
  }
}

  5. Browser submits the profile to Kratos: POST /self-service/registration?flow=<id>.

    Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

csrf_token=<token>
&traits.email=test@test.com
&traits.name.first=Test1
&traits.name.last=Test
&method=profile

  6. Kratos checks the profile, then changes the form stored in the flow for the next screen: the profile fields become hidden and a password field is added. It redirects back to the UI: /registration?flow=<id>. No account is created yet. Answering a form post with a redirect is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern, so a page refresh does not resubmit the form.

  7. UI fetches the flow again and shows the password form. The profile values are now hidden fields:

    "nodes": [
  { "attributes": { "name": "csrf_token", "type": "hidden", "value": "<token>" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.email", "type": "hidden", "value": "test@test.com" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.first", "type": "hidden", "value": "Test1" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.last", "type": "hidden", "value": "Test" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "password", "type": "password", "required": true } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "method", "type": "submit", "value": "password" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "screen", "type": "submit", "value": "previous" } }
]

  8. Browser submits the password to Kratos, with the profile again: POST /self-service/registration?flow=<id>.

    csrf_token=<token>
&traits.email=test@test.com
&traits.name.first=Test1
&traits.name.last=Test
&password=<password>
&method=password

  9. Kratos checks the input, creates the identity and a session, starts email verification, and redirects (303 See Other) to the UI's verification page with the session cookie:

    HTTP/1.1 303 See Other
Location: http://127.0.0.1:4455/verification?flow=2f6c3de3-1d88-4dfd-916b-fedc463f39f7
Set-Cookie: ory_kratos_session=<session>; …

  10. UI shows the verification form. The user is now logged in.

    participant B as Browser

    B->>UI: GET /registration

    K-->>B: 303 → /registration?flow=id

    UI->>K: GET /self-service/registration/flows?id=id

    B->>K: POST /self-service/registration (method=password)
    K->>DB: save identity + credential
    K->>DB: save session
    K->>DB: save verification flow, queue email
    K-->>B: 303 → /verification?flow=vid, session cookie
    B->>UI: GET /verification?flow=vid
    UI-->>B: verification form

docs.title: Server-driven UI
docs.text:
Kratos decides what the form contains, and the UI only draws it. Each flow carries ui.nodes (UI nodes), a list of fields with name, type, required flag, value and error messages, plus ui.action and ui.method for where to post. The UI loops over the nodes and renders them. It controls only layout and styling.

This keeps the rules in one place. A new trait in the identity schema (a JSON Schema), or a new method such as passkeys, shows up in every UI without UI changes. Web, mobile and single-page apps render the same nodes. Kratos checks every submit against the flow it stored, so a client cannot skip a step. Errors come back as the same flow with messages on the fields. The cost is flexibility: a fully custom sign-up sequence is harder, because Kratos decides the steps.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is when another site makes the user's browser send a request the user did not intend. Without protection, another site could post a sign-up form to Kratos from the user's browser. The browser would follow the redirect and store the session cookie, so the user would be logged in to an account the attacker created and controls. Anything the user then enters goes into the attacker's account. This is called login CSRF.

To block this, Kratos requires a secret that only the user's browser holds, and checks that every form post carries it. This is the double-submit cookie pattern:

  • Secret. On the first request from a browser with no CSRF cookie (step 3, GET /self-service/registration/browser), Kratos generates a random secret and stores it in an HttpOnly cookie named csrf_token_<hash>. It is one secret per browser, kept across flows.
  • Form field. Whenever Kratos builds a form (step 3, and again in step 6), it puts a copy of the secret in the hidden csrf_token field. The copy is masked with fresh random bytes each time, which is why the field value differs between steps 5 and 8. Masking protects against BREACH, an attack that recovers a secret repeated unchanged in compressed HTTPS responses.
  • Check. On each submit (steps 5 and 8), Kratos unmasks the field and compares it with the cookie. If they don't match, the post is rejected.

Another site can make the browser send the cookie, but the same-origin policy stops it from reading the cookie or the form, so it cannot fill in the field.

API flows for native apps use no cookies, so they skip this check. Instead, Kratos rejects an API flow request that carries cookies or an Origin header, since that means it came from a browser.

docs.title: Have I Been Pwned
docs.text:
Kratos rejects passwords that have already leaked in a data breach, because attackers try those first, for example in credential stuffing. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2 requires this: a new password SHALL be compared against a blocklist that includes passwords from previous breaches. Kratos asks Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), using its Pwned Passwords API, without ever sending the password: it asks for a bucket of leaked passwords that look alike, then searches the bucket itself.

This runs on the password submit (step 8), after the length check (at least 8 characters) and a check that the password is not too similar to the email (by Levenshtein distance and longest common substring):

  1. Kratos hashes the password with SHA-1. password becomes 5BAA61E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8.
  2. It sends only the first 5 characters: GET https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/5BAA6.
  3. HIBP returns every leaked hash starting with that prefix, as suffix and count. For 5BAA6, that was 1,977 lines on 2026-10-11, including 1E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8:52372427.
  4. Kratos looks for its own suffix in the list. If the count is above max_breaches (default 0), the password is rejected with an error on the password field.

Hundreds of passwords share each prefix, so HIBP cannot tell which one was checked. This technique is called k-anonymity; Cloudflare describes its design for HIBP. SHA-1 is used only because the HIBP dataset is indexed by it; the stored password is hashed separately with bcrypt. If HIBP is unreachable, Kratos accepts the password (ignore_network_errors defaults to true). This is a fail-open choice: an outage does not block sign-ups, but the leak check is skipped.
